transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

Not necessarily. A heat-pump dryer is meant to run much cooler and slower than an older condenser dryer, so it may feel only mildly warm in the first half hour. Towels are also one of the slowest loads. Around 3½ hours can be normal on an energy-saving cotton/towel programme, particularly if the load is large or not well spun first. It becomes more suspicious if the towels are still properly damp at the end of a full cycle, rather than simply taking longer than the old machine. A heat-pump fault is less likely from temperature alone; a failed system is usually genuinely cold and repeatedly leaves laundry wet. 1. With the dryer switched off, clean the door lint filter and the lower heat-exchanger/second filter if it has one. Remove all fluff gently; rinse only if the instructions allow it, then refit it properly. Restricted filters can add a lot of time.
2. Try one normal, well-spun towel load: no more than roughly two-thirds of the drum, using the full cupboard-dry or extra-dry setting rather than iron-dry or Eco. Empty the water tank first if the dryer uses one. This gives the sensor the best chance of judging dryness correctly. If it still leaves that test load wet after a complete cycle with clean filters, it is reasonable to contact the retailer/manufacturer while it is only about a month old. They would need to assess the airflow, moisture sensing and, if necessary, the sealed heat-pump circuit; that last part is not a DIY repair.

Right ok. The towels do come out fully dry in the end, it just takes ages. I clean the fluff filters after every load and cleaned the other filter about two weeks ago and it looked clean. I use Cotton Cupboard Dry with a full drum, and I open the door two or three times to check on it. Does any of that matter?

Yes—both matter. A full drum of towels is about the hardest case for a heat-pump dryer: towels hold a lot of water and need room for air to circulate. Filling it to around two-thirds rather than completely full can make a noticeable difference. Opening the door two or three times also extends the run. Each time, the warm air escapes and the dryer has to rebuild its working temperature and humidity conditions; it is not a sign of a fault that it feels only mildly warm when checked early on. At present this sounds more like normal heat-pump behaviour than a failed part, because the load does finish fully dry. The main alternatives are towels going in too wet from the washer, or a less obvious airflow restriction, but regular filter cleaning makes the latter less likely. 1. Try one comparison load: washer on its highest suitable spin, dryer no more than about two-thirds full, Cotton Cupboard Dry, and keep the door shut. This is the most useful test of whether load size/wetness is causing the long time.
2. If that load is dry in substantially less time, there is no fault—use smaller loads for towels and avoid interrupting the cycle.
3. If it still takes around 3½ hours despite that, clean the deeper filter again exactly as the manual specifies and make sure it is fully seated. If performance then worsens, or loads start ending damp, contact the manufacturer/retailer while the machine is still very new; they can assess the airflow and heat-pump system. There is no reason yet to suspect or replace a component.

candidates: Normal lower-temperature heat-pump drying, especially on an Eco/cotton towel programme (high)
Restricted airflow from lint or heat-exchanger filters (medium)
Laundry entering too wet, a large load, or programme/dryness setting (medium)
